explanations.E0050:
# E0050: a type that cannot be inferred

`None` takes the optional type its position expects. Where nothing says which type, Sisu cannot choose one.

## Why

Every optional is an optional of some type: `None` of `i64?` and `None` of `Tree?` are different values. A `let` with no type has nothing to take it from.

A call of a generic function, class or variant has the same problem when nothing fixes one of its type parameters. `first([])` gives `T` no type: the `[]` has none of its own, and a later use of the result does not count. Annotate the result, `let x: i64? = first([])`, or write the type arguments, `first<i64>([])`. A parameter that the result names only through an associated type, as `S` in `-> [S.Item]`, is not fixed by an annotation of the result: write the type arguments, `collect<Countdown>()`.

An alias whose body does not use a type parameter has the same problem. In `type F<T> = f64`, no value gives `T` a type, so the compiler cannot infer `T` at `F.pi`. Write the type argument, `F<i64>.pi`, or remove `T` from the alias, `type F = f64`. Sisu gives no warning for a type parameter that nothing uses.

`Some(None)` has the same problem: `Some` holds a value of any type, and `None` has no type of its own. Annotate the optional, `let x: i64?? = Some(None)`.

`Ok(1)` has the same problem: `Ok` holds the value, and nothing says the type of the error. Annotate the result, `let r: Result<i64, string> = Ok(1)`. `Err("bad")` leaves the type of the value open in the same way.

`x ?? None ?? 0` has the same problem, because `??` groups to the right. It is `x ?? (None ?? 0)`, and nothing gives that `None` a type. To remove two layers from an `i64??`, write `(x ?? None) ?? 0`.

## Broken

```sisu
fn main() {
    let x = None
}
```

## Fixed

```sisu
fn main() {
    let x: i64? = None
    print(x ?? 0)
}
```
explanations.W0015:
# W0015: optional that `print` or an interpolation may write as `None`

The warning is for an optional that `print`, `eprint` or an interpolation writes as text. An optional can be `None`, and then the program writes the word `None`. The program still builds. The warning is at the optional itself. The message names it with its path (`name`, `user.name`). When the optional has no path (`find()`, `xs[0]`), the message says "this value". The message reads `` `name` can be `None`, and then this writes the word "None" ``. The help names the three fixes.

## Why

A program that writes `Hello None` has a bug that no error shows. The warning is there so that you choose what the program writes when the value is missing. Three fixes are possible:

- Unwrap the optional with `if let`, and write only when the value is there.
- Give a default with `??`.
- Call `to_string()` on the optional, to write `None` on purpose.

An optional that sits inside another value gets no warning. An array of optionals, the payload of an enum and the optional inside an optional all print the way their code reads (`[1, None]`). A call of `to_string()` does not warn either. A generic function that prints a value of type `T` does not warn, also when `T` is an optional where it is called. A `Some(x)` is never `None`, and gets no warning.

A precision on an optional is not a warning. It is the error [E0111](E0111.md). A part whose format spec has an error gets no warning either: the spec error is its one report.

## Broken

```sisu
fn main() {
    let name: string? = "Sisu"
    print("Hello {name}")
}
```

## Fixed

```sisu
fn main() {
    let name: string? = "Sisu"
    print("Hello {name ?? "friend"}")
}
```
